title: Vercel Functions now support request bodies up to 20MiB
summary:
Vercel Functions now accept inbound request bodies up to 20MiB, up from 4.5MB, in Public Beta.

To turn this on, set the VERCEL_SUPPORT_LARGE_REQUEST_BODY=1 environment variable. The opt-in applies to the whole project in the environment where you set it, so you can test the larger limit on preview before enabling it in production. It requires the project's functions to use the performance memory setting of 4GB. It applies to functions on the Node.js, Python, and Bun runtimes, and to Routing Middleware. Functions and Routing Middleware on the Edge runtime keep the 4.5MB cap and return 413 on oversize bodies, so moving them onto the larger limit means switching to the Node.js runtime with runtime: 'nodejs', or proxy.ts in Next.js.

When a project opts in, Routing Middleware receives request headers and metadata but no request body, enforced at the project level. Middleware still runs and still sees every other request header, so body-dependent middleware behavior is the one thing that becomes unavailable. This avoids sending the body twice, to both middleware and the target function, which would raise cost and time to first byte.

When handling larger request bodies, read the body promptly and avoid holding it in memory to prevent backpressure and memory issues.

Learn more in the Vercel Functions limitations documentation.

title: Vercel completes ISO/IEC 42001:2023 certification
summary:
Vercel has completed its ISO/IEC 42001:2023 certification, meeting the international standard for AI management systems.

This certification gives our customers confidence to ship fast with agents on Vercel, demonstrating how Vercel designs, builds, operates, and governs our AI products.

Our AI management system covers Vercel’s underlying infrastructure and core AI products, including AI Gateway, Vercel Agent, v0, AI-based open source software and frameworks, as well as the people and processes behind them.

Vercel’s certificate is available here, and additional audit documentation is available through our Trust Center.

What is ISO 42001?

ISO/IEC 42001:2023 is the international standard for AI management systems and applies to any organization that develops, provides, or uses AI.

An AI management system is the set of policies, roles, processes, and controls through which an organization consistently governs AI activities. The standard includes requirements for leadership accountability, AI risk assessment, lifecycle management, data governance, transparency, and continual improvement.

The requirement that makes ISO 42001 distinct from security standards is the AI system impact assessment. Security frameworks cover how an organization protects information, but ISO 42001 covers how it builds and uses AI, including the assessment of how an AI system impacts the people it touches, and the benefits and harms that would result when that system materially changes.

To obtain the certification, we underwent a two-stage audit performed by an independent, accredited certification body, which evaluated whether our AI management system is designed correctly and operates effectively. The certificate is valid for three years, with annual surveillance audits in between.

“Enterprises want agents in production, but no one should have to choose between moving fast with AI and governing it well,” said Talha Tariq, CTO for Security. “We built our AI governance to run as continuously as we ship, and ISO 42001 is the independent check that it works.”

What this means for customers

AI moved into the critical path of how software gets built faster than the governance around it did. Teams are shipping agents, assistants, and model-backed features on Vercel every day, and the questions that follow are no longer hypothetical:

  • Who is accountable when a model behaves unexpectedly?

  • What data reached a model?

  • How is the system monitored once it’s live?

  • Who decided the system was ready?

We pursued ISO 42001 because we are committed to providing enterprise-grade AI products. This certification attests that we run deliberate, auditable AI systems.

How we govern AI at Vercel

There are three primary ways AI is governed at Vercel.

Impact assessments

Vercel conducts AI system impact assessments which cover foreseeable benefits, harms, failures, and misuse. We reassess these risks and benefits when the system materially changes.

Evaluations before release

We maintain evals for our AI systems covering performance, safety, and security, with human review for material changes.

Clear data commitments

Where it is not the default option based on pricing plan, we provide customers the ability to set their data handling preferences ranging from zero data retention (ZDR) to training opt-out. Our AI policy is available at v0.app/policy.

Ship fast, with confidence

We are committed to helping teams ship fast with confidence in the way AI is built and governed at Vercel. ISO 42001 is proof of that commitment, giving our customers:

  • Confidence in agentic infrastructure: Vercel’s AI systems have been audited, which means customers using our AI products start from a reviewed foundation instead of an unexamined one.

  • Governance can ship at the speed of the product: Agents now drive the development and deployment of applications. Governance and oversight that occurs quarterly can’t govern software that changes hourly, so we built a system that reviews AI as continuously as we ship it.

  • Simplified and accelerated assurance: Customers and partners can rely on this certification, alongside our other compliance attestations, to meet AI governance diligence requirements for faster third-party vendor onboarding.

  • Clear lines of responsibility: ISO 42001 requires that responsibilities be allocated across the AI supply chain. Our documentation outlines what Vercel is accountable for and what remains yours, the same shared-responsibility model we use for security.

  • Discipline that holds over time: Annual surveillance audits mean this isn’t a one-time claim. As our AI products change, the system that governs them stays under independent review.

AI is changing what people build on Vercel, and we intend for the governance around it to keep pace. We’ll continue to expand the scope of our certifications as our products grow.

title: Agents can now find Vercel CLI commands by describing the task
summary:
Coding agents can now use vercel help search to find Vercel CLI commands by describing a task in plain language.

The search returns a list of matching commands. Add --with-help to include the help page for the first result in the same call. For example, vercel help search "roll back production" --with-help returns the options and examples for vercel rollback.

Search also supports:

  • API endpoints: When a Vercel API endpoint matches the task, search returns a vercel api command with the request path and placeholders for every required input. The agent can fill in the values without guessing the path.

  • JSON output: Use --json to return search results as JSON. Combine it with --with-help to include usage instructions, options, and examples for the first result.

Search recognizes common wording, such as “show” instead of “list,” and handles minor spelling mistakes.

The CLI also includes a skill that tells coding agents to start with vercel help search when looking for a command. Vercel doesn't log your search text.

Update to the latest Vercel CLI with vercel upgrade.

title: Vercel Billing CLI is now available
summary:
You can now check your team’s billing overview, review and download invoices, and preview upcoming charges with the Vercel CLI. All billing commands, including usage and budgets, are now grouped under vercel billing.

Billing overview and invoice history are available on all plans, subject to your team’s existing billing permissions. Upcoming invoice estimates require an active paid subscription.

Billing overview

Check your team’s plan, billing status, billing cycle, balance due, and overdue invoices:

In CLI 65.17.0 and later, this overview also includes configured invoice details such as your billing address, tax ID, and purchase order.

Invoices and upcoming charges

Use vercel billing invoices to review invoices, download PDFs, and preview upcoming charges. For inspect and download, replace with a full invoice ID from the list output:

Upcoming charges are estimates and may change until the end of the billing period.

For scripts and agents, add --json to vercel billing overview or any vercel billing invoices subcommand for structured output.

Existing usage and budget commands now also use the same prefix:

  • vercel usage → vercel billing usage

  • vercel budgets → vercel billing budgets

The previous command names continue to work as aliases.

To get started, update your Vercel CLI with vercel upgrade. Learn more in the Billing & Invoices documentation.

title: Priority Projects now in public beta
summary:
Priority Projects are now in public beta for Pro and Enterprise teams. This optional upgrade for individual Vercel projects adds bot and traffic-source signals, Page Integrity for monitoring and controlling client-side scripts and connections, and additional Firewall controls and alerts.

Bot signals

Bot protection is free on all plans. You can enable it to challenge non-browser traffic while allowing verified bots. Priority adds more detailed bot signals: categories, verification status, and names where available. Use these signals in:

  • Firewall rules: Match on bot_name, bot_category, bot_status, and bot_protection in the dashboard or with vercel firewall rules add.

  • Application code: Read x-vercel-bot-category, x-vercel-bot-name, and x-vercel-verified-bot from request headers in Routing Middleware and Vercel Functions. See the header reference for verified and claimed bot names.

  • Logs and Observability: Logs show the Firewall action on all plans. Priority adds the matched rule and bot details where available. In Firewall Observability, Priority adds botCategory for unverified traffic. Log Drains also include bot classifications.

Traffic Sources

Priority adds Traffic Sources labels for requests from Tor exit nodes, VPNs, open or anonymizing proxies, and residential proxies. It also labels traffic flagged by abuse blocklists.

Use these labels in custom Firewall rules, analyze them in Firewall Observability, or read them from the x-vercel-waf-source request header in your application. A request can have multiple labels.

Use the Traffic Sources managed ruleset to log, challenge, or block traffic by source category. Review matching traffic before enabling blocking, since these categories can also include legitimate users.

To enable the Traffic Sources managed ruleset from the CLI, run vercel firewall managed-rulesets enable traffic-sources. This stages the change; review it with vercel firewall diff, then apply it with vercel firewall publish.

Page Integrity

Priority Projects get access to Page Integrity to monitor client-side scripts and connections, receive alerts when new scripts or connections are detected, and block unapproved resources.

Page Integrity maintains a resource inventory and uses Content Security Policy (CSP) for discovery and enforcement, without adding client-side JavaScript.

It operates in three stages:

  • Detect: Discover scripts using report-only CSP headers on sampled requests.

  • Review: Approve or reject scripts and record business justifications.

  • Block: Enforce a CSP that blocks scripts outside the approved inventory.

Page Integrity must be enabled separately. Configure monitoring and review resources in the dashboard; the CLI can also show its resource inventory:

Firewall controls and alerts

Anomaly alerts

DDoS alerts are available on all plans. Priority adds anomaly alerts for bot traffic and requests matching system or custom Firewall rules. Use these alerts to investigate potential attacks and unusual traffic patterns.

Configure notifications in your team’s Settings > Alerts, with delivery options including email, Slack, and webhooks.

View recent alerts with vercel alerts --since 24h. To manage alert configuration from the CLI, see vercel monitors.

OWASP Core Ruleset

On Pro, Priority lets you enable the OWASP Core Ruleset to protect against common web application attacks. Enterprise projects can already enable it without Priority.

Add it as a team default from Security > Rules, or enable it for a linked project via the CLI with vercel firewall managed-rulesets enable owasp --yes followed by vercel firewall publish. OWASP inspection is billed separately per inspected request and GB of inspected payload.

Response-based rate limiting

Priority adds response conditions to the rate-limit rules available on all plans. Count requests toward a limit only when their responses match specified HTTP status codes or response headers. For example, count 401 responses from failed login attempts or 404 responses for missing pages, rather than every matching request.

Higher Firewall limits

Get started

Priority costs $200 per project per month. Enable it from your project’s Firewall or Settings page, or with the CLI.

For the CLI, update to the latest version with vercel upgrade, then enable Priority for the project you want to upgrade:

Page Integrity usage is billed separately. Its standard rate is $2 per 1,000 monitored page views, with each view covering up to 100 scripts.

Learn more in the Priority Projects documentation.

title: Introducing Vercel Board
summary:
Software development is moving from individual agents completing tasks to teams of agents working on more complex projects.

A single agent can track its work in a Markdown file, but there isn't a purpose-built primitive for tracking tasks, delegation, statuses, logs, and completed work across many agents and subagents.

We ran into this coordination problem internally and started experimenting with a shared message board as a primitive on two key projects:

  • Our security agents: We deployed a swarm of agents to analyze our codebases for vulnerabilities, push fixes and updates, and now we keep track of their work via Board.

  • v0's software factory: After seeing how well Board worked for security agents, we rebuilt v0's software factory on it, and it now merges over 50% of PRs.

Along the way, we added multiple features like grants for different levels of access (for humans and agents), two-way sync for multiple tools (like Slack), and a lot more.

Today we are launching Vercel Board as an experimental agentic primitive. It packages what we've learned about coordinating work across agent fleets and builds towards a future where multiple teams of humans and agents orchestrate swarms, software factories, and other agentic workflows.

We built Board for our own needs, but invite curious developers to test it alongside us and give feedback. It is harness agnostic and fits well into existing multi-agent reinforcement learning. Claude Code, Codex, Pi, OpenCode, eve, fx, Mastra, and LangChain can collaborate as if they were a single harness.

How it works

title: Introducing Vercel X
summary:
Today we’re launching Vercel X, a six-week accelerator for AI founders at the idea and pre-seed stages.

Join a cohort of 40 teams at our San Francisco HQ and build alongside Vercel’s product leaders, designers, and engineers.

The program takes no equity for participation and offers access to a program-wide pool of more than $9M in credits from Vercel, AWS, Anthropic, OpenAI, and other partners.

Applications are now open through November 29, 2026. The program runs from January 19 to March 2, 2027.

Vercel has worked with more than 100 early-stage teams from around the world across three accelerator cohorts. Alumni include Rex, Alloy Robotics, Interfaze, Cervo, and Hacktron. Interfaze and Rex are backed by Y Combinator, and Cervo was acquired by Altana Technologies.

Why Vercel X?

If you’re applying to Vercel X, you probably have an idea or project you haven’t been able to stop thinking about. The next stretch is figuring out exactly what you’re building and who it’s for.

We think you get through that stretch the Vercel way: by deeply understanding your customers, shipping quickly, and iterating to greatness.

The program includes:

  • Technical mentorship: Hands-on workshops and product feedback from Vercel’s design, product, and engineering teams.

  • Partner credits: Put credits toward hosting, compute, and model API usage as you build and test your product.

  • Founder community: A cohort of AI founders at the same stage, with weekly fireside chats featuring industry leaders.

  • Investor access: Mentorship from VC partners and the opportunity to present your company to investors, ecosystem partners, and the Vercel community at Demo Day.

Winning teams receive funding from Vercel Ventures and prizes from program partners.

Who should apply

We’re looking for technical builders with ambitious ideas and insatiable curiosity.

You don’t need a finished product or traction. Tell us what you want to build, who needs it, what AI makes possible, and why you’re the right person or team for the job.

Solo founders and teams of up to three can apply from around the world. You must be a Vercel customer and must not have participated in a traditional VC accelerator or raised an institutional seed round. See the additional eligibility requirements below.

All participants must spend the full six weeks in San Francisco and attend weekly events in person.

Apply to Vercel X

Applications close at 11:59 p.m. PT on Sunday, November 29, 2026. Decisions will be released in mid-December.

Apply to Vercel X →

Applicants must be Vercel customers at or above the age of majority in their jurisdiction, able to commit to the full six weeks in person, and not located in or otherwise subject to restrictions imposed by U.S. sanctions laws.

Vercel X program applications will be judged on the quality of the submission, the founder's background, and the overall potential for impact.

title: Vercel Blob now supports TTLs for automatic deletion
summary:
Vercel Blob can now delete blobs automatically. Pass ttlDays when you write a blob and it is deleted that many days after upload, from 1 to 730 days. The TTL counts from the blob's upload date.

Use TTLs for blobs you would otherwise delete yourself, such as session transcripts, exports, and temporary uploads.

ttlDays works on put(), copy(), putImage(), multipart uploads, and presigned upload URLs. Every write result and head() response now includes expiresAt, so you know when a blob is due for deletion.

setTtl() changes or removes the TTL of blobs you already have, one URL or up to 1,000 at a time, without re-uploading them.

In Vercel CLI 65.16.0 and later, pass --ttl-days to vercel blob put, put-image, copy or presign, and use vercel blob set-ttl on existing blobs.

Setting a TTL costs one Advanced Operation per started 60 days, on top of the write. A 7-day TTL costs one, and the 730-day maximum costs 13. Clearing a TTL and the deletions themselves are free. You can track TTL operations in the Blob section of the Observability tab.

npm install @vercel/blob@2.9.0

Learn more in the Vercel Blob documentation.

summary:
Speed Insights now measures soft navigations: client-side route changes that update page content without a full reload. This means you can now track performance as users move through your app, not just on full-page loads.

Speed Insights captures LCP, FCP, INP, and CLS for soft navigations and includes these measurements in your Real Experience Score. TTFB is not captured because there is no new document request.

Soft-navigation tracking is enabled by default for all projects using Speed Insights, with no action required. It works with modern web frameworks such as Next.js, SvelteKit, and Nuxt, in Chromium-based browsers.

In your project's Speed Insights dashboard, use the new Navigation Type filter to view All, Hard, or Soft navigation data.

Soft-navigation events count toward Speed Insights Plus usage. For existing projects that had Plus enabled before this release, Speed Insights events from soft navigations will not be charged until December 1. For projects that newly enable Plus, these events are billed from the start.

title: Decision-1.1 now available on AI Gateway
summary:
Decision-1.1 from Microsoft AI is now available on AI Gateway. It is more accurate, better calibrated, and faster than Decision-1.

The decision model returns structured answers instead of free-form text for tasks such as routing support requests, choosing which model should handle a request, selecting the next step in a workflow, or grading AI responses.

  • Boolean: the probability that a condition is true

  • Choice: a selected category and probabilities for each option

  • Score: a numerical rating on a scale you define

Multiple questions can share the same input in one request. Better calibration means the model's probabilities track how often it is right, so your application can set thresholds for when to act, flag a case for review, or escalate.

Decision-1.1 accepts the same request format as Decision-1. To switch, change the model ID to microsoft/decision-1.1.

Call it through the AI SDK, the OpenAI-compatible Decisions API, or the AI CLI. The examples below require ai 7.0.128 or later for TypeScript, or the OpenAI Python SDK 3.26.0 or later for Python.

Decision requests appear in request logs, count toward budgets, and support decision fallbacks.

Try Decision-1.1 in the model playground, or see the decision models documentation for request formats and question types.

title: Agents are users, so your software needs evals
summary:
Agents are now users of software, doing work on people's behalf. Whether you're building the agent or the software it uses (API, CLI, MCP server, SDK), evals give you a way to measure how well that work gets done.

Agents probably missed your launch video and billboard on Highway 101, but they still go through the same funnel a human does to find and use a product: Discovery, Selection, Access, and Success.

You can build evals for any stage of this funnel. Here, we’ll focus on the final stage, Success: whether the agent completes the user’s task correctly.

That's more difficult to check than it sounds. An agent can place a “successful” order for a hot latte when the user asked for an iced one. The request worked, so the logs in your Observability stack look fine. And because LLM outputs vary between runs, one good manual test can’t tell you whether a fix worked. You need to repeat the same tasks and grade the outcomes, before and after the change.

That’s what an eval is, a test you run many times and score. Here’s how we build one.

The agentic testing pyramid

If a test asks “did it work?”, an eval asks “how often does it work, and how well?”

We group agentic software tests by how many LLM calls they typically need: deterministic tests (0), one-turn evals (1), and E2E evals (2+ across a whole task). This has turned out to be a great proxy for the effort to build them, the time they take to run, and the cost of running them. Just like in the practical test pyramid, the cheap and fast tests should make up the bulk of your test suite.

To use the pyramid, start with the problem you want to catch and pick the lowest tier that can catch it. For Success, that's the top. A one-turn eval checks a single decision, like which command the agent runs first. But Success depends on the whole sequence of steps (e.g. search for cafes → filter on user criteria → place the latte order). Each one can look reasonable on its own, and the agent can still get the wrong outcome.

An E2E eval lets the agent work through the whole task in an environment, then checks whether the final result meets the user’s requirements. You’ve probably seen a few already; most popular coding benchmarks, like SWE-bench and Terminal-Bench, are E2E evals.

Example

Say you own SF Beans, an API for ordering coffee in San Francisco. One of the best ways to give agents access to your service is through a CLI, so you’re shipping sfbeans.

Here’s a typical request from one of your customers:

Get me a large iced latte with whole milk, ready for pickup by 9:00, under $8 including tip. I’m in the Mission.

Here’s what sfbeans knows at 8:30am:

  • Fog City Roasters: ice machine is down, so no iced drinks today (temperature)

  • 24th St Beans: latte is $7.50 on the menu, but $9.27 after tax and tip (budget)

  • Dolores Drip: latte is $5.50, but the earliest pickup is 9:20 (time)

  • Valencia Grind: $7.42 after tax and tip, ready at 8:50 (meets all three)

Here’s what you could test at each layer of the pyramid for sfbeans:

How to build an end-to-end eval

We’ll build the coffee eval with Harbor, an open-source framework from the creators of Terminal-Bench that runs agents in containers, checks results, and records their actions.

Here are the terms we’ll use:

  • Task: one problem for the agent to solve, with a starting environment and a way to check whether it succeeded

  • Variant: the agent setup you’re testing, like the model, prompt, tools, memory and skills

  • Trial: one attempt by one variant at one task

  • Run (a job in Harbor): every variant tried on every task, several times each

  • Trace (a trajectory in Harbor): everything recorded during a trial: messages, tool calls, logs, files and final output

Step 1: Set a goal

Building E2E evals for everything isn’t practical. With traditional software, you can aim for 100% test coverage. With agents, the surface you’d need to cover is everything an LLM might do with your product, and even figuring out where that ends is hard (see the jagged frontier).

Start with one outcome your users care about, narrow enough to evaluate with a handful of tasks. You’ll usually find that goal in one of three places:

  • Observability: which agents use your product, and where they fail

  • Customers: support tickets, feedback, and churn

  • Roadmap: the product hypotheses you most need to validate

For example, your goal might be to:

  • Increase the success rate on a specific task

  • Reduce the number of steps required to accomplish a goal

  • Check whether an agent skill helps, and get feedback to improve it

  • A/B test a prompt

  • Explore the frontier by checking whether a use case is achievable with current LLMs, and if they fail, why

Example

We looked in all three places for sfbeans:

  • Observability: Most agent traffic comes from Claude Code and Codex. We know because sfbeans adds a user-agent header when it detects a specific coding harness.

  • Customers: The top support ticket is “my agent ordered the wrong drink”: a hot latte instead of iced, a pickup after the user’s meeting, or a total over budget once tax and tip are added.

  • Roadmap: Nothing urgent, so the wrong-drink problem goes first, since it drives churn.

That gives us our goal:

Goal

Increase the success rate on ordering the exact drink the user asked for

Agents

Claude Code and Codex, since that’s where our traffic comes from.

In scope

Drink, pickup time, and budget (incl. tax and tip), using today’s sfbeans.

Out of scope

Cancellations, refunds, and accounts. We’ll eval those later.

Done when

Both agents get the order right in every trial, not just most of the time.

Step 2: Define metrics

Here are the metrics we use most for E2E agent evals:

Success

  • Success rate: the share of trials that pass

  • Pass@k: the chance that at least one of k trials passes (answers “can the agent do this at all?”)

  • Pass^k: the chance that all k trials pass (answers “can I rely on it every time?”)

Efficiency (measured on successful trials only)

  • Steps: the number of agent turns needed to complete the task

  • Time: how long the trial took

  • Cost: how much the trial cost, in dollars

Example

Our goal is to get every order right in every trial. Once we build and run the eval in Steps 3 and 4, here’s what five trials of Claude Code + Opus 5.5 (anthropic/claude-opus-5.5 on AI Gateway) on the iced latte order could look like:

What the numbers mean:

  • Success rate: 3 of 5 trials passed, so 60%.

  • Pass@5: Assuming independent trials with a 60% success rate, 1 − 0.4^5 ≈ 99%. Give the agent 5 tries and it almost certainly gets it right once.

  • Pass^5: 0.6^5 ≈ 8%. The chance the agent gets 5 orders in a row right.

  • Steps: (9 + 11 + 8) / 3 ≈ 9 on successful trials. The failed trials are shorter because the agent skipped work, like quoting, which is why efficiency only counts successful trials.

  • Time: ~3:50 on successful trials.

  • Cost: $0.56 per successful trial, but $2.35 / 3 = $0.78 per success once you count the failed trials you paid for too.

So does Opus work? Its 99% pass@5 says yes. Its 8% pass^5 says a user who orders this every weekday gets at least one wrong coffee in 92% of weeks. Both numbers are right. They just answer different questions: pass@5 asks whether the agent can get the order right, and pass^5 asks whether it gets it right every time.

Which metric matters most depends on what a failure costs your user. Someone ordering their morning coffee doesn’t get a retry. If the agent orders a hot latte, or one that’s ready after their train leaves, they’ve paid for the wrong coffee and started their day annoyed. They need it right every morning, so sfbeans optimizes for pass^5.

Other products are more forgiving, because a failed attempt is cheap and gets caught before it matters:

Overall averages can hide a task that fails frequently, so always inspect results per task. And with only five trials, 100% means “no failures seen yet,” not “never fails.”

Step 3: Design the task set

In Step 1, we set a goal for the eval: increase how often agents order the exact drink the user asked for. But an agent can’t attempt a goal. It needs a task: one concrete request, drawn from what your users actually ask for.

Pick tasks hard enough that you learn something from running them. A good set covers the common case, the edge cases that trip agents up, and at least one request where the right move is not to act.

For each task, define these parts:

  • An instruction: the user’s request

  • An environment: where the agent works, with the same starting state for every trial

  • A verifier: a check of the final state, ideally scored per constraint

  • A known-good solution (optional): a reference run that demonstrates the expected behavior and passes the verifier

You can make every aspect of that environment as fake or as realistic as you need, depending on your goals. The OpenPipe team has a nice writeup on how they defined the environment for an email research agent.

Example

We wrote four tasks, each one a Harbor task folder in tasks/.

  • Common case: iced-latte-mission, the order from earlier

  • Edge case: usual-unavailable, where the user’s usual cafe is out of their drink

  • Edge case: team-order, with 6 drinks, $45 total, and one pickup spot

  • Don’t act: impossible-request, where nothing fits, so the right move is to tell the user

impossible-request has one extra check. Its verifier reads a command log the agent can’t write to, to confirm the agent searched before giving up. We learned we needed that the hard way (see Step 5).

Here’s iced-latte-mission:

The instruction gives the agent the user’s request and names the sfbeans CLI. In production, agents find the tool through a skill, docs, or an MCP server. Naming it here skips Discovery and Selection, keeping the eval focused on Success.

We also specify that it’s 8:30am. Only sfbeans uses our frozen clock; the sandbox’s system clock still shows the real time:

The environment is part real, part fake. The agent uses the real sfbeans CLI, but against seeded cafes and a frozen clock, so every trial starts on the same morning:

To keep the demo simple, cafes.json lives inside the agent’s environment. In a real eval, protect the seed data and verifier code, and make sure the agent can update order records only through the CLI. Agents can attempt to reward hack if it helps them pass, for example by editing the inventory or writing orders.json directly.

For this coffee order, the verifier checks the final order against the user’s requirements. Harbor runs test.sh after the agent finishes and reads the scores it writes to /logs/verifier/reward.json:

The actual check lives in check_orders.py. It scores each constraint separately, then sets reward to 1 only if all of them pass. Harbor uses reward as the trial’s main score:

The solution is a known-good answer. Run it before any real agent to prove the task works:

Finally, task.toml ties the task together. It sets the timeouts, runs the verifier in the agent’s sandbox (where orders.json lives), and saves the orders as an artifact so we can inspect them in Step 5:

Step 4: Run the eval

If you share the universal distaste for slow CI, you’ll hate waiting for evals. Every trial waits on an agent making LLM calls, step after step, and a run repeats that for every variant and task, several times each.

Harbor’s Vercel integration, which we built upstream, speeds that up a lot. It runs trials concurrently, each in its own Vercel Sandbox, and caches built task environments so they aren’t rebuilt for every trial. Routing model calls through AI Gateway gives you one key and one budget across model providers.

Example

Two agents, Claude Code and Codex, with two models each, make four variants.

Then install Harbor, connect a Vercel project, and run the job:

This run fits on the Hobby plan: 10 concurrent sandboxes is the Hobby limit, and each trial is well under its 45-minute session cap. On Pro, you can raise n_concurrent_trials as high as 10,000 (Sandbox limits).

To keep the example simple, we pass the OIDC token into each sandbox as an env var, where the agent can read it. Beyond a demo, use short-lived tokens, and use Harbor’s Vercel integration to set Sandbox firewall rules that lock each trial down to only the hosts it needs, like AI Gateway.

Internally, we go a step further and use credentials brokering to attach credentials to outgoing requests, keeping API keys outside the agent’s environment.

Step 5: Analyze traces

Now for the meaty part: trace-diving. Scores tell you how often your agents fail; traces tell you why. Read the failures, and some passes too, since a pass only means the verifier was satisfied.

Example

The run from Step 4 leaves 80 trial folders in jobs/sfbeans-baseline/. Each has the trial’s result, the agent’s trajectory, the verifier’s scores, and, because task.toml saves it as an artifact, the order the agent placed:

Run harbor view jobs to browse the results. Here’s what our four variants could report (numbers are illustrative).

For each variant, we calculate success rate and estimate pass^5 separately for each task, then average each metric across the four tasks. Each task counts equally.

That’s our baseline. On pass^5, the metric we chose in Step 2, even the best variant is far from reliable. But the score doesn’t tell us what to fix. For that, we have to open the failed trials.

Take trial 2 from Step 2. Claude Code + Opus 5.5 ordered at 24th St Beans for $9.27. The verifier tells us which constraint it broke:

Right drink, on time, over budget, and the saved orders.json confirms the $9.27 total. Now we read agent/trajectory.json. The agent searches for lattes in the Mission, sees $7.50 on the menu, and goes straight to order. No quote. It treated the menu price as the final price.

Trial 1, from the same variant, quotes three cafes, rules out 24th St Beans, and orders at Valencia Grind for $7.42. So the CLI can get the order right, but the agent doesn’t reliably check the total before spending the user’s money.

We then look for that pattern across other failed trials, and if it keeps showing up, we have something specific to fix: make the total harder to miss, or add a --max-total flag so order refuses anything over budget. That’s a much more useful conclusion than “Opus scored 85%.”

When we first ran this demo, the traces also exposed problems with what the eval was measuring:

  • Our first run scored 0% on every variant. The agents didn’t know sfbeans existed, so they never tried it (obviously). That’s the funnel’s Discovery stage failing in our own eval. Naming the tool in the instruction fixed it, and it’s a good reminder that being discoverable is part of your product. In the wild, that’s the job of your skill, docs, MCP server and AEO.

  • Codex kept looking for sfbeans as a connected tool and never tried running it in the shell. That’s an Access problem, not a Success one.

  • Codex passed impossible-request almost every time, but when we read the traces, 9 out of 10 passes were the agent giving up without looking. The verifier only checked that no order was placed, so we tightened it to also check that the agent searched first. Without reading the traces, we’d have counted those as wins.

Automated trace analysis

For larger runs, inspecting every trial by hand gets slow, so we automate it.

Up to 40 reader agents running fast models like deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash read trial transcripts in parallel and summarize their findings. A smarter coordinator agent reviews those summaries, sends readers back for more context when needed, and writes the final report. An analysis.md file tells the coordinator what to look for, so we can reuse the workflow across runs.

Model calls go through AI Gateway. Trial artifacts stay in Vercel Drives during analysis, and traces go to Vercel Blob for long-term storage.

Iterate to greatness

Your first eval run gives you a baseline. Now act on it.

Pick the fix the traces point to, like the --max-total flag, rerun the same job, and compare against the baseline. Check whether it reduces the targeted failures without introducing new ones, then use those results to decide whether the change is ready to ship.

Once you’ve built an eval, it keeps paying off for a lot of different things. Rerun it on every release to catch regressions; test prompt, skill, and model changes before shipping; learn how agents use your product; or build auto-optimization loops on top of it.

Expect to add harder tasks over time. As models and your product improve, evals saturate, meaning agents start passing every task. A saturated eval still catches regressions, but it can’t tell you what to improve next.

Evals are the infrastructure you use to make your product better, again and again. Vercel has the pieces you need to build them in one place: AI Gateway for model calls across providers, Sandbox to run trials at scale, and Drives and Blob to keep every trace.

  • Time: how long the trial took

  • Cost: how much the trial cost, in dollars

So does Opus work? Its 99% pass@5 says yes. Its 8% pass^5 says a user who orders this every weekday gets at least one wrong coffee in 92% of weeks. Both numbers are right. They just answer different questions: pass@5 asks whether the agent can get the order right, and pass^5 asks whether it gets it right every time.

Which metric matters most depends on what a failure costs your user. Someone ordering their morning coffee doesn’t get a retry. If the agent orders a hot latte, or one that’s ready after their train leaves, they’ve paid for the wrong coffee and started their day annoyed. They need it right every morning, so sfbeans optimizes for pass^5.

Overall averages can hide a task that fails frequently, so always inspect results per task. And with only five trials, 100% means “no failures seen yet,” not “never fails.”

Step 3: Design the task set

In Step 1, we set a goal for the eval: increase how often agents order the exact drink the user asked for. But an agent can’t attempt a goal. It needs a task: one concrete request, drawn from what your users actually ask for.

Pick tasks hard enough that you learn something from running them. A good set covers the common case, the edge cases that trip agents up, and at least one request where the right move is not to act.

For each task, define these parts:

  • An instruction: the user’s request

  • An environment: where the agent works, with the same starting state for every trial

  • A verifier: a check of the final state, ideally scored per constraint

  • A known-good solution (optional): a reference run that demonstrates the expected behavior and passes the verifier

You can make every aspect of that environment as fake or as realistic as you need, depending on your goals. The OpenPipe team has a nice writeup on how they defined the environment for an email research agent.

Example

We wrote four tasks, each one a Harbor task folder in tasks/.

  • Common case: iced-latte-mission, the order from earlier

  • Edge case: usual-unavailable, where the user’s usual cafe is out of their drink

  • Edge case: team-order, with 6 drinks, $45 total, and one pickup spot

  • Don’t act: impossible-request, where nothing fits, so the right move is to tell the user

impossible-request has one extra check. Its verifier reads a command log the agent can’t write to, to confirm the agent searched before giving up. We learned we needed that the hard way (see Step 5).

We also specify that it’s 8:30am. Only sfbeans uses our frozen clock; the sandbox’s system clock still shows the real time:

The environment is part real, part fake. The agent uses the real sfbeans CLI, but against seeded cafes and a frozen clock, so every trial starts on the same morning:

To keep the demo simple, cafes.json lives inside the agent’s environment. In a real eval, protect the seed data and verifier code, and make sure the agent can update order records only through the CLI. Agents can attempt to reward hack if it helps them pass, for example by editing the inventory or writing orders.json directly.

For this coffee order, the verifier checks the final order against the user’s requirements. Harbor runs test.sh after the agent finishes and reads the scores it writes to /logs/verifier/reward.json:

The actual check lives in check_orders.py. It scores each constraint separately, then sets reward to 1 only if all of them pass. Harbor uses reward as the trial’s main score:

The solution is a known-good answer. Run it before any real agent to prove the task works:

Finally, task.toml ties the task together. It sets the timeouts, runs the verifier in the agent’s sandbox (where orders.json lives), and saves the orders as an artifact so we can inspect them in Step 5:

Step 4: Run the eval

If you share the universal distaste for slow CI, you’ll hate waiting for evals. Every trial waits on an agent making LLM calls, step after step, and a run repeats that for every variant and task, several times each.

Harbor’s Vercel integration, which we built upstream, speeds that up a lot. It runs trials concurrently, each in its own Vercel Sandbox, and caches built task environments so they aren’t rebuilt for every trial. Routing model calls through AI Gateway gives you one key and one budget across model providers.

Then install Harbor, connect a Vercel project, and run the job:

This run fits on the Hobby plan: 10 concurrent sandboxes is the Hobby limit, and each trial is well under its 45-minute session cap. On Pro, you can raise n_concurrent_trials as high as 10,000 (Sandbox limits).

To keep the example simple, we pass the OIDC token into each sandbox as an env var, where the agent can read it. Beyond a demo, use short-lived tokens, and use Harbor’s Vercel integration to set Sandbox firewall rules that lock each trial down to only the hosts it needs, like AI Gateway.

Internally, we go a step further and use credentials brokering to attach credentials to outgoing requests, keeping API keys outside the agent’s environment.

Step 5: Analyze traces

Now for the meaty part: trace-diving. Scores tell you how often your agents fail; traces tell you why. Read the failures, and some passes too, since a pass only means the verifier was satisfied.

Example

The run from Step 4 leaves 80 trial folders in jobs/sfbeans-baseline/. Each has the trial’s result, the agent’s trajectory, the verifier’s scores, and, because task.toml saves it as an artifact, the order the agent placed:

Run harbor view jobs to browse the results. Here’s what our four variants could report (numbers are illustrative).

That’s our baseline. On pass^5, the metric we chose in Step 2, even the best variant is far from reliable. But the score doesn’t tell us what to fix. For that, we have to open the failed trials.

Take trial 2 from Step 2. Claude Code + Opus 5.5 ordered at 24th St Beans for $9.27. The verifier tells us which constraint it broke:

Right drink, on time, over budget, and the saved orders.json confirms the $9.27 total. Now we read agent/trajectory.json. The agent searches for lattes in the Mission, sees $7.50 on the menu, and goes straight to order. No quote. It treated the menu price as the final price.

Trial 1, from the same variant, quotes three cafes, rules out 24th St Beans, and orders at Valencia Grind for $7.42. So the CLI can get the order right, but the agent doesn’t reliably check the total before spending the user’s money.

We then look for that pattern across other failed trials, and if it keeps showing up, we have something specific to fix: make the total harder to miss, or add a --max-total flag so order refuses anything over budget. That’s a much more useful conclusion than “Opus scored 85%.”

When we first ran this demo, the traces also exposed problems with what the eval was measuring:

  • Our first run scored 0% on every variant. The agents didn’t know sfbeans existed, so they never tried it (obviously). That’s the funnel’s Discovery stage failing in our own eval. Naming the tool in the instruction fixed it, and it’s a good reminder that being discoverable is part of your product. In the wild, that’s the job of your skill, docs, MCP server and AEO.

  • Codex kept looking for sfbeans as a connected tool and never tried running it in the shell. That’s an Access problem, not a Success one.

  • Codex passed impossible-request almost every time, but when we read the traces, 9 out of 10 passes were the agent giving up without looking. The verifier only checked that no order was placed, so we tightened it to also check that the agent searched first. Without reading the traces, we’d have counted those as wins.

Automated trace analysis

For larger runs, inspecting every trial by hand gets slow, so we automate it.

Up to 40 reader agents running fast models like deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash read trial transcripts in parallel and summarize their findings. A smarter coordinator agent reviews those summaries, sends readers back for more context when needed, and writes the final report. An analysis.md file tells the coordinator what to look for, so we can reuse the workflow across runs.

Model calls go through AI Gateway. Trial artifacts stay in Vercel Drives during analysis, and traces go to Vercel Blob for long-term storage.

Iterate to greatness

Your first eval run gives you a baseline. Now act on it.

Pick the fix the traces point to, like the --max-total flag, rerun the same job, and compare against the baseline. Check whether it reduces the targeted failures without introducing new ones, then use those results to decide whether the change is ready to ship.

Once you’ve built an eval, it keeps paying off for a lot of different things. Rerun it on every release to catch regressions; test prompt, skill, and model changes before shipping; learn how agents use your product; or build auto-optimization loops on top of it.

Expect to add harder tasks over time. As models and your product improve, evals saturate, meaning agents start passing every task. A saturated eval still catches regressions, but it can’t tell you what to improve next.

Evals are the infrastructure you use to make your product better, again and again. Vercel has the pieces you need to build them in one place: AI Gateway for model calls across providers, Sandbox to run trials at scale, and Drives and Blob to keep every trace.

title: Vercel Sandbox Python SDK 1.0 is now available
summary:

The SDK includes context managers for automatic sandbox cleanup and AnyIO-based async support for asyncio and Trio. For synchronous code, use vercel.sandbox.sync.

Install with uv add 'vercel-sandbox>=1.0' and configure authentication.

If you’re upgrading from 0.x, review the 1.0 release notes for breaking changes, including the switch to bytes for command input and output.

title: Daemons can now send traces to Vercel Tracing
summary:
Vercel Daemons can now send OpenTelemetry traces to Vercel Tracing, allowing you and your agents to inspect background worker operations alongside the rest of your project's traces.

Vercel provides each daemon with a Unix socket for receiving OTLP/HTTP traces and sets the socket's path in VERCEL_OTEL_SOCKET_PATH.

Upgrading @vercel/otel to version 2.3.0 or later enables automatic trace export for Node.js daemons using the default configuration. The SDK detects this socket and sends the spans your worker records to Vercel.

These spans are available through the Vercel CLI, which can search by service name within a project and return JSON for your agents.

Learn more in the daemon tracing documentation.
